dublinCore.description: Interactive comparison of sine, square, triangle and sawtooth waves: a 50 ms window of the waveform in the time domain on top and its harmonic line spectrum from 0 to 500 Hz below, with each line scaled relative to the fundamental, so students can see which harmonics each shape contains and how fast they decay.

learningObjectives: Compare the harmonic spectra of sine, square, triangle and sawtooth waves at the same fundamental frequency
Explain why square and triangle waves contain only odd harmonics while sawtooth waves contain every integer harmonic
Distinguish the 1/n amplitude decay of a square wave from the 1/n^2 decay of a triangle wave in the spectrum plot
Predict how raising the fundamental frequency slider rescales the position of every harmonic line
Relate jumps and corners of a waveform in the time domain to the amount of high-frequency energy in its spectrum
prerequisites: Frequency and period of a sinusoid

misconceptions.misconception: Harmonics are extra tones that the analyser adds to every signal
misconceptions.correction: Harmonics are part of the waveform's shape; a pure sine has none
misconceptions.evidence: Select Sine: only one line appears at the slider frequency, whatever the frequency

misconceptions.misconception: Square and triangle waves have the same spectrum because both contain only odd harmonics
misconceptions.correction: The lines sit at the same frequencies but decay at different rates, 1/n versus 1/n^2
misconceptions.evidence: At 100 Hz the 3rd harmonic is 0.333 of the fundamental for the square wave and 0.111 for the triangle wave

accessibility.screenReaderScript: Waveform type FFT analysis. The top plot shows 50 milliseconds of a sine, square, triangle or sawtooth wave; the bottom plot shows its harmonic spectrum from 0 to 500 Hz, with each line scaled relative to the fundamental. Choose the waveform with the radio buttons and set the fundamental frequency with the slider.

controls.label: Waveform
controls.description: Selects the waveform shape: Sine, Square, Triangle or Sawtooth

controls.label: Frequency
controls.description: Sets the fundamental frequency f of the waveform

visualElements.description: Time-domain plot (green): 50 ms of the waveform with amplitude gridlines at +1 and -1, a 10 ms time grid, and a read-out of the period T = 1/f

Frequency-domain plot (purple): one line per harmonic from 0 to 500 Hz, height relative to the fundamental, labelled with its harmonic number; hovering a line highlights it in gold and shows its frequency and magnitude
Harmonic-content summary (for example 'Odd harmonics, 1/n decay') and the frequency read-out

model.description: Generates one of four periodic waveforms of peak amplitude 1 and plots the magnitudes of its Fourier-series harmonics up to 500 Hz, divided by the magnitude of the fundamental.
equations: square(t) = (4/pi) sum over odd n of sin(n w t)/n
triangle(t) = (8/pi^2) sum over odd n of (-1)^((n-1)/2) sin(n w t)/n^2
sawtooth(t) = (2/pi) sum over n >= 1 of (-1)^(n+1) sin(n w t)/n
relative magnitude: sine 1 (n = 1 only); square 1/n (odd n); triangle 1/n^2 (odd n); sawtooth 1/n (all n)
harmonic frequency f_n = n f, period T = 1/f
algorithms: Analytic Fourier-series line spectrum (equivalent to the peak heights of an ideal FFT over a whole number of periods)
limitations: The spectrum is computed from the Fourier series, not by running an FFT on samples, so it shows no leakage, windowing or aliasing
Magnitudes are relative to each waveform's own fundamental, so the absolute difference between waveforms (4/pi for the square, 8/pi^2 for the triangle, 2/pi for the sawtooth) is not shown
The triangle and sawtooth are drawn starting from -1, a time shift that changes only the phases of the harmonics, not their magnitudes

instructionalStrategies: Predict-then-verify: predict which harmonic lines appear before switching the waveform
Compare-and-contrast square and triangle waves at the same frequency
Read exact magnitudes by hovering over a line
extensions: Add audio output so students can hear the timbre of each waveform
Add a dB (logarithmic) magnitude scale to make the small triangle-wave harmonics visible
Add partial-sum reconstruction to show the Gibbs phenomenon
